raw_response.country: Multiple low- and middle-income countries (primarily African and Southeast Asian regions across 20 included studies)

criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1: The scoping review focuses exclusively on institutional environmental health services within healthcare facilities (719 hospitals and health centers), not household or community water or sanitation service access, and examines CQI process implementation rather than service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper touches on institutional and administrative implementation factors such as Ministry of Health leadership, local government coordination, and facility-level team decision-making autonomy (so it could be viewed as broadly touching institutional/governance factors under the plain reading, though the overall paper would still be excluded for failing C1 and C4). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, it fails C2 because WASH FIT is a participatory continuous quality improvement (CQI) and facility management/project-delivery tool, not a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies C3: Systematic scoping review synthesizing 20 peer-reviewed and grey-literature empirical/programmatic implementation studies identified via structured database and repository searches with dual-reviewer screening and extraction.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails C4: Extracts and reports only implementation process indicators (which of the five WASH FIT cycle steps were completed, adaptation archetypes, stakeholder roles, and self-reported implementation facilitators/barriers). It reports no water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (explicitly noting that WASH FIT effectiveness on WASH services was examined in a separate review).
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies C5: Population/unit of analysis (719 healthcare facilities across 20 studies in LMICs), intervention/exposure (implementation and adaptation of the WHO/UNICEF WASH FIT continuous quality improvement cycle), process outcomes (completion/adaptation of the 5 WASH FIT steps and implementation practices), and study design (systematic scoping review) are clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies C6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: WASH FIT is a risk-based, continuous quality improvement tool that aims to help healthcare facilities plan, prioritize, implement, and monitor improvements to environmental health services using a participatory approach

Our specific research objectives were to (1) describe contexts and stakeholders involved in WASH FIT implementation, (2) describe the WASH FIT process and identify any adaptations, and (3) assess good practices for implementing WASH FIT.
Across all studies, WASH FIT was implemented in 719 healthcare facilities, with an average of 36 facilities per study (ranging from 1 to 256).

WASH FIT programs were mostly led by Ministries of Health or similar health-related government agencies (e.g., national public health institutes and regional health departments), with 14 studies (70%) reporting leadership or substantial involvement from the government.
To describe WASH FIT processes, we extracted data on which of the five WASH FIT cycle steps a study completed, plus any additional steps not described in the official WASH FIT manual.

raw_response.exposure: Implementation and adaptation of the WHO/UNICEF Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT) five-step continuous quality improvement cycle
raw_response.outcome: Completion and adaptation of the five WASH FIT implementation steps (assessors vs. improvers archetypes) and qualitative implementation facilitators/barriers (no WASH service access outcomes reported)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 719 healthcare facilities (hospitals and health centers) across 20 included studies in low- and middle-income countries
raw_response.rationale: The retrieved OA PDF is the 2024 medRxiv preprint version of the exact same study (matching title and authors). Full-text review shows that this systematic scoping review must be excluded under both the narrow rule-type and plain readings of Criterion 2: (1) Wrong population/setting (E02, failing C1): it examines institutional environmental health management in healthcare facilities (719 hospitals and health centers) rather than household or community water or sanitation service access; (2) Wrong exposure (failing C2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type reading): WASH FIT is a facility-level participatory continuous quality improvement (CQI) and program-delivery tool rather than a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism governing service access; and (3) Wrong outcome (failing C4): it synthesizes only CQI process fidelity, step adaptations, and implementation best practices, reporting no water or sanitation access outcomes.
